abstract: ILO research brief for International Women's Day 2026. It applies the ILO-NASK global index of occupational exposure to generative AI (Gmyrek et al., 2025) to the ILO's harmonized microdata on the gender composition of employment in 84 countries. The brief finds that female-dominated occupations, concentrated in business administration and clerical support, are almost twice as likely to be exposed to Gen AI as male-dominated ones (29 versus 16 per cent). They also face much higher automation risk: 16 per cent of female-dominated occupations sit in the two highest exposure gradients, against 3 per cent of male-dominated ones. Women are more exposed than men in 88 per cent of countries in the sample. Exposure also varies with income level: 41 per cent of employment is potentially exposed in high-income countries against 11 per cent in low-income countries, and 9.6 per cent of high-income employment sits in the highest-automation gradient 4 against 0.3 per cent in low-income countries. The ILO argues that the wider impact of Gen AI lies in job quality (task reshaping, work intensity, autonomy, bias) more than in job counts.
keyFindings: 29% of female-dominated occupations and 28% of mixed occupations are exposed to Gen AI, compared with 16% of male-dominated occupations (global, 436 ISCO-08 occupations)
16% of female-dominated occupations fall in exposure gradients 3–4 (highest automation risk), versus 13% of mixed and 3% of male-dominated occupations

Women are more exposed to Gen AI than men in 88% of the 84 countries in the sample; over 40% of female employment is exposed in some Pacific and Caribbean small island states, Switzerland, the UK, Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Philippines
41% of employment is potentially exposed to Gen AI in high-income countries versus 11% in low-income countries; 9.6% of high-income employment is in gradient 4 versus 0.3% in low-income countries
Of 436 occupations, 82 (19%) are female-dominated, 89 (20%) male-dominated and 266 (61%) mixed
Women made up 30% of the AI workforce in 2022, about 4 percentage points more than in 2016 (WEF data cited by the ILO)
methodology: Applies the ILO-NASK task-based global index of occupational exposure to Gen AI (Gmyrek et al., 2025; tasks scored through worker surveys, expert validation and AI modelling, aggregated to 4-digit ISCO-08 and classed into gradients 1–4) to ILO harmonized microdata on employment by sex in 84 countries (latest year available per country). Female-dominated occupations: female share of at least 75% in at least 25% of countries; male-dominated: female share below 25% in the same proportion of countries (Hegewisch and Liepmann, 2013). An occupation enters only if at least nine countries report it.
qualifiers: Tier 2: international organization research brief, not peer-reviewed. Exposure is potential task overlap, not displacement; the ILO states that exposure does not necessarily mean job redundancy and that even gradient-4 automation should not be assumed. The 29/16 comparison counts occupations, not workers, and the brief notes it captures only part of employment exposure. Global and cross-country: no US-specific estimate, and the US is not called out in the country results. The 41% high-income exposure figure differs from the 34% high-income share in the May 2025 ILO-NASK paper, though both cite Gmyrek et al. (2025). Country data vary in reference year. Secondary figures (AI workforce share, STEM shares) come from WEF, LinkedIn and ILOSTAT, not the ILO's own analysis.
